tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: SuggestPluginInstall

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__update_plan
tools.description:
Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

Never spend a message on this tool alone: send it IN THE SAME MESSAGE as another tool call (in parallel), so it costs no extra round trip.
- First call: with the VERY FIRST tool call of the turn, even one that only reads or lists files: {"items": [...]}, the whole plan in order, short imperative phrases (at most ~7 words, no numbering), the step you are starting "in_progress", the rest "pending". If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.
- Out of order: {"done": [2], "start": 4} (1-based).
- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields — recap and ask are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label and message are the user's words back to you:
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

recap.description: Two or three short sentences to the user (≤300 chars): what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified. Its first sentence is the sidebar status. It must stand on its own, since it is also read away from the transcript and the box draws under anything you write after this call: never point at anything else in the conversation ("listed below", "see above", "in my message").

ask.description: The one question (≤100 chars) when the next move is the user's call — a choice, a go-ahead (to act here on what this turn found, say), an approval: the decision alone, with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give (actions[0] is your pick). Like the recap, never point at anything else in the conversation. Omit it, and actions, when nothing waits on the user.

blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

action.description: An app action update_plan's result listed as available now, or one your own work this turn made available; anything else is refused, and one that stops being available later is dropped (as actions[0], with your ask and the other answers), so do not guess. Omit for a reply.

label.description: For a reply: the button text, 1–3 words (4 only when three cannot say it) / 24 characters — "Yes, fix 1", "Fix 2 instead", "Not now": a button, not a sentence; the detail goes in message. No leading / or !. Ignored for an app action (the app's own label is used).

message.description: For a reply: what the click sends, up to 300 characters of plain text — no leading / or !. Omit when the label is the whole message.

actions.description: 1–2 buttons, recommendation first. They are answers to your ask: the first accepts your recommendation, and another is there only when it is a realistic alternative the user might pick instead — not a menu of everything you mentioned. When blocked is true, they are the most likely answers to your question. While Auto-fix is on for the session's PR, none offers to watch it, fix CI, resolve conflicts or address comments.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

For computer items whose action is left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key or type, and for form_input items, include action_summary in the item's input, as you would when calling that tool directly.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

content.text:
Yes, it returns the **whole `PropertySpace` objects**. `.Where(...)` only decides which items to keep and doesn't trim them down to just the colour. Here's each step with example data.

## Example board (`_spaces`)

```csharp
_spaces = new List<Space>
{
    new GoSpace       { Name = "GO" },
    new PropertySpace { Name = "The Burvale",       Price = 1, Colour = "Brown" },
    new PropertySpace { Name = "Fast Kebabs",       Price = 2, Colour = "Brown" },
    new PropertySpace { Name = "The Grand Tofu",    Price = 3, Colour = "Red"   },
    new PropertySpace { Name = "Lanzhou Beef Noodle", Price = 3, Colour = "Red" },
};
```

## Calling `ColourGroup("Brown")`

**Step 1: `.OfType<PropertySpace>()`** drops `GoSpace` and keeps only the property spaces:

```
[ The Burvale (1, Brown), Fast Kebabs (2, Brown), The Grand Tofu (3, Red), Lanzhou Beef Noodle (3, Red) ]
```

**Step 2: `.Where(space => space.Colour == "Brown")`** keeps the items where the condition is `true`. Each item is kept whole:

```
[ The Burvale (1, Brown), Fast Kebabs (2, Brown) ]
```

**Step 3: `.ToList()`** turns the result into a `List<PropertySpace>`:

```
List<PropertySpace> (Count = 2)
[0] → PropertySpace { Name = "The Burvale", Price = 1, Colour = "Brown" }
[1] → PropertySpace { Name = "Fast Kebabs", Price = 2, Colour = "Brown" }
```

So you can use every property on the results:

```csharp
var browns = ColourGroup("Brown");
foreach (var p in browns)
    Console.WriteLine($"{p.Name} - ${p.Price} - {p.Colour}");
// The Burvale - $1 - Brown
// Fast Kebabs - $2 - Brown
```

## Two things worth knowing

1. **The list holds references, not copies.** These are the same objects that are in `_spaces`. If you change `browns[0].Price = 99`, the property on the board changes too. That's usually what you want, for example when you check ownership of the whole colour group.

2. **Getting only part of the object needs `.Select`.** `.Where` filters and `.Select` reshapes:

   ```csharp
   _spaces.OfType<PropertySpace>()
          .Where(s => s.Colour == colour)
          .Select(s => s.Name)      // now only the names come back
          .ToList();                // List<string> { "The Burvale", "Fast Kebabs" }
   ```

To see it yourself, set a breakpoint on the `return` line, step over it, and hover over the result in the debugger. Or print it with:

```csharp
ColourGroup("Brown").ForEach(p => Console.WriteLine($"{p.Name}, {p.Price}, {p.Colour}"));
```

content.text:
Yes. `space` is a `PropertySpace`. `ColourGroup(...)` returns a `List<PropertySpace>`, so `.All(space => ...)` hands you one `PropertySpace` at a time, and `space` is just the name for the current item.

## The question this code answers

**"Does the owner of this property own every property of the same colour?"** If they do, the rent is doubled.

## Example

Say Bob lands on **Fast Kebabs**, and Alice owns it.

```
property = Fast Kebabs (2, Brown)
owner    = Alice   // found earlier with _owners.TryGetValue(property, out var owner)
player   = Bob
```

**Step 1:** `_board.ColourGroup("Brown")` returns:

```
[ Fast Kebabs (2, Brown), jamai (1, Brown) ]
```

**Step 2:** `.All(...)` runs the check on each space and returns `true` only if **every** check is `true`.

## Scenario A: Alice owns both

```
_owners = { Fast Kebabs → Alice, jamai → Alice }
```

| `space` | `TryGetValue` finds it? | `groupOwner` | `groupOwner == owner`? | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Fast Kebabs | true | Alice | Alice == Alice → true | **true** |
| jamai | true | Alice | Alice == Alice → true | **true** |

`All` → **true**, so `ownsGroup = true`, and rent = 2 × 2 = **4**.

## Scenario B: jamai is unowned

```
_owners = { Fast Kebabs → Alice }
```

| `space` | `TryGetValue` finds it? | `groupOwner` | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fast Kebabs | true | Alice | **true** |
| jamai | **false** (not in the dictionary) | null | **false** |

`All` → **false**, so rent = 2 × 1 = **2**.

## Scenario C: Charlie owns jamai

```
_owners = { Fast Kebabs → Alice, jamai → Charlie }
```

| `space` | found? | `groupOwner` | `== Alice`? | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Fast Kebabs | true | Alice | true | **true** |
| jamai | true | Charlie | **false** | **false** |

`All` → **false**, so rent = **2**.

## Why both parts of the `&&` are there

```csharp
_owners.TryGetValue(space, out var groupOwner) && groupOwner == owner
```

1. **`TryGetValue(space, ...)`** asks "does anyone own this space?" and, if someone does, puts that player in `groupOwner`.
2. **`groupOwner == owner`** asks "is that person the same owner?"

If part 1 is `false`, `&&` stops there and part 2 never runs, so an unowned space makes the check fail.

## The same logic as a plain loop

If the one-liner is hard to read, this does exactly the same thing:

```csharp
bool ownsGroup = true;
foreach (PropertySpace space in _board.ColourGroup(property.Colour))
{
    if (_owners.TryGetValue(space, out var groupOwner))   // is it owned?
    {
        if (groupOwner != owner)       // owned, but by someone else
        {
            ownsGroup = false;
            break;
        }
    }
    else                               // not owned by anyone
    {
        ownsGroup = false;
        break;
    }
}

var rent = property.Price * (ownsGroup ? 2 : 1);
owner.Receive(player.Pay(rent));   // Bob pays, Alice receives
```

Like the loop's `break`, `.All` stops as soon as it finds one `false`.

content.text:
If `_board[4] is not PropertySpace property` gives **false**, that means `_board[4]` **is** a `PropertySpace`. In that case `property` holds that same object, now typed as `PropertySpace`, so you can use `.Name`, `.Price` and `.Colour`.

## What the line does

```csharp
if (_board[player.Position] is not PropertySpace property) return;
```

This is a pattern match that does two jobs at once:

1. **It checks the type.** Is the space at this position a `PropertySpace`?
2. **It casts and assigns.** If it is, the object goes into a new variable `property` of type `PropertySpace`.

The `not` flips the result so the method can exit early when the space is not a property.

## Example

```
_board[0] = GoSpace       { Name = "GO" }
_board[1] = PropertySpace { Name = "The Burvale", Price = 1, Colour = "Brown" }
...
_board[4] = PropertySpace { Name = "Fast Kebabs", Price = 2, Colour = "Brown" }
```

### `player.Position = 4`

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| `_board[4] is PropertySpace` | true |
| `is not PropertySpace` | **false**, so no `return` |
| `property` | `PropertySpace { Name = "Fast Kebabs", Price = 2, Colour = "Brown" }` |

The code continues, and `property.Price` is `2`, `property.Colour` is `"Brown"`, and so on. It's the same object as `_board[4]`, not a copy.

### `player.Position = 0`

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| `_board[0] is PropertySpace` | false (it's a `GoSpace`) |
| `is not PropertySpace` | **true**, so `return` |
| `property` | not assigned. The method exits, so you never get to use it. |

## Why it's useful

`_board[i]` is typed as the base class `Space`, which has only `Name`. Writing `_board[4].Price` won't compile. The pattern gives you a variable of the right type.

## The same logic written the long way

```csharp
Space current = _board[player.Position];

if (!(current is PropertySpace))
    return;                                  // GO or another non-property space

PropertySpace property = (PropertySpace)current;   // safe cast
// property.Name, property.Price, property.Colour are now available
```

The one-line version does the check, the cast and the assignment together. The compiler also knows that `property` is assigned only when the code gets past the `return`, so you can use it safely below that line.

content.text:
Small mix-up here: when the condition is **false**, the `return` does **not** run. An `if` runs its statement only when the condition is **true**.

```csharp
if (condition) return;
//  true  → return runs, the method exits
//  false → return is skipped, the code carries on to the next line
```

## When `property` gets set

`property` is set whenever the object **is** a `PropertySpace`. The type check happens first, and the assignment is part of that check:

```
_board[4] is PropertySpace property
   │
   ├─ Is it a PropertySpace?  YES → property = _board[4]  (set here)
   │                                result = true
   └─ Is it a PropertySpace?  NO  → property is not set
                                    result = false
```

Then `not` flips the result, and the `if` decides whether to `return`.

## Position 4 (a PropertySpace)

1. `_board[4] is PropertySpace property` → **true**, and **`property = Fast Kebabs`** is assigned here.
2. `not true` → **false**.
3. `if (false) return;` → the return is **skipped**.
4. The code continues, and `property` holds Fast Kebabs.

## Position 0 (GO)

1. `_board[0] is PropertySpace property` → **false**, and `property` is not assigned.
2. `not false` → **true**.
3. `if (true) return;` → the method **exits**.
4. `property` is never used, so it doesn't matter that it wasn't set.

## Summary

| Space | is a `PropertySpace`? | `property` set? | `if` condition (`is not`) | `return` runs? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `_board[4]` Fast Kebabs | yes | **yes** | false | **no**, the code continues |
| `_board[0]` GO | no | no | true | **yes**, the method exits |

So whenever the code gets past this line, `property` is guaranteed to hold a valid `PropertySpace`. The line works as a guard: "if this isn't a property, leave; otherwise, here it is as `property`."

content.text:
`is not` is evaluated in two parts. First it checks whether the object is a `PropertySpace` (and assigns `property` if it is). Then `not` flips that answer.

```csharp
_board[player.Position] is not PropertySpace property
//                      └─┬─┘ └─┬┘ └──────┬──────────┘
//                        │     │         └ pattern: "is a PropertySpace? if yes, call it property"
//                        │     └ not: flip the match result
//                        └ is: test the value against the pattern
```

## Step by step

**Step 1: get the value.**
`_board[player.Position]` → for example, the object at index 4.

**Step 2: test the inner pattern `PropertySpace property`.**
- Is the object a `PropertySpace` (or a class derived from it), and not `null`?
  - **Yes:** the pattern matches, and the object is assigned to `property`.
  - **No:** the pattern doesn't match, and nothing is assigned.

**Step 3: apply `not`.**
- If the pattern matched → `not` gives **false**.
- If the pattern didn't match → `not` gives **true**.

**Step 4: the `if` acts on that result.**
- **true** → `return`.
- **false** → skip the return and continue with `property` ready to use.

## What the compiler turns it into

Under the hood the compiler produces roughly this:

```csharp
PropertySpace property = _board[player.Position] as PropertySpace;
if (property == null) return;
```

`as` tries the cast and gives `null` if the object isn't a `PropertySpace`. So:

| `_board[i]` | `as PropertySpace` gives | `== null`? | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fast Kebabs (`PropertySpace`) | the Fast Kebabs object | false | continue, `property` = Fast Kebabs |
| GO (`GoSpace`) | `null` | true | `return` |
| `null` (an empty slot) | `null` | true | `return` |

## Why the compiler allows you to use `property` afterwards

The compiler tracks when `property` is **definitely assigned**:

- `x is PropertySpace p` → `p` is assigned when the result is **true**.
- `x is not PropertySpace p` → `p` is assigned when the result is **false**.

Your `if` returns when the result is true, so the only way to reach the next line is the false path, where `property` is assigned. That's why this compiles:

```csharp
if (_board[player.Position] is not PropertySpace property) return;
Console.WriteLine(property.Price);   // OK: property is assigned here
```

But this doesn't, because there's no guard:

```csharp
var ok = _board[player.Position] is not PropertySpace property;
Console.WriteLine(property.Price);   // error CS0165: use of unassigned local variable 'property'
```

`TryGetInt32` isn't anywhere in this folder, so this is the general explanation. It's most likely from reading JSON files such as `board.json` and the rolls files.

## What it is

`TryGetInt32` is a method on **`JsonElement`** (from `System.Text.Json`). It works like `TryGetValue`: it tries to read a JSON value as an `int` and tells you whether that worked.

```csharp
bool ok = element.TryGetInt32(out int value);
```

- If the JSON value is a whole number that fits in an `int`, it returns **`true`**, and `value` holds the number.
- If it isn't (a decimal, too large, or the wrong kind of number), it returns **`false`**, and `value` is `0`.

`Int32` is just .NET's name for `int` (a 32-bit integer).

## Example with a Monopoly board

`board.json`:

```json
[
  { "name": "GO", "type": "go" },
  { "name": "The Burvale", "price": 1, "colour": "Brown", "type": "property" },
  { "name": "Fast Kebabs", "price": 2.5, "colour": "Brown", "type": "property" }
]
```

Reading it:

```csharp
using var doc = JsonDocument.Parse(File.ReadAllText("board.json"));

foreach (JsonElement item in doc.RootElement.EnumerateArray())
{
    if (item.TryGetProperty("price", out JsonElement priceElement) &&
        priceElement.TryGetInt32(out int price))
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"{item.GetProperty("name").GetString()} costs {price}");
    }
    else
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"{item.GetProperty("name").GetString()} has no valid price");
    }
}
```

What happens for each item:

| Item | `TryGetProperty("price")` | `TryGetInt32` | Output |
|---|---|---|---|
| GO | **false** (no `price` key) | not run (`&&` stops) | has no valid price |
| The Burvale | true, element is `1` | **true**, `price = 1` | costs 1 |
| Fast Kebabs | true, element is `2.5` | **false** (not a whole number), `price = 0` | has no valid price |

There are two "Try" steps here:
1. **`TryGetProperty`** asks whether the key exists. It's like `TryGetValue` on a dictionary.
2. **`TryGetInt32`** asks whether the value is a valid `int`.

## `TryGetInt32` vs `GetInt32`

| Method | When the value isn't a valid int |
|---|---|
| `GetInt32()` | **throws** an exception (`FormatException`) |
| `TryGetInt32(out int x)` | returns **false**, no exception |

```csharp
int a = priceElement.GetInt32();          // crashes on 2.5
bool ok = priceElement.TryGetInt32(out int b);   // ok = false, b = 0
```

## One catch

`TryGetInt32` works only when the JSON value is a **number**. If it's a string, such as `"price": "1"`, calling it throws an `InvalidOperationException` instead of returning `false`. You can check the kind first:

```csharp
if (priceElement.ValueKind == JsonValueKind.Number &&
    priceElement.TryGetInt32(out int price))
{
    // safe
}
```

## The "Try" pattern

All of these follow the same idea: return a `bool` and give the result through `out`.

| Method | Tries to… |
|---|---|
| `dictionary.TryGetValue(key, out v)` | find a key in a dictionary |
| `int.TryParse("42", out n)` | turn a **string** into an int |
| `element.TryGetProperty("x", out e)` | find a key in a JSON object |
| `element.TryGetInt32(out n)` | read a JSON **number** as an int |

content.text:
You've got the first part right. If the property **is** in the dictionary, `TryGetValue` returns `true` and `owner` is set. Then `!` flips that `true` to **`false`**, so the `if` block is **skipped**, and the code continues to the next line with `owner` ready to use.

`!` means "not". It only flips the `bool`. It doesn't change `owner`.

```
TryGetValue(...)   →  true    (owner = Alice)
!true              →  false
if (false) { ... }  →  block skipped
```

## Both cases

```csharp
if (!_owners.TryGetValue(property, out var owner))
{
    // runs only when the property is NOT owned yet
    var paid = player.Pay(property.Price);
    if (paid == property.Price) _owners[property] = player;
    return;
}
if (owner == player) return;
// ...rent code below
```

### Case 1: the property is unowned (`_owners` is empty)

| Step | Value |
|---|---|
| `TryGetValue` | **false**, `owner = null` |
| `!false` | **true** |
| `if` block | **runs**: the player pays, `_owners[property] = player`, then `return` |

The method ends inside the block, so `if (owner == player)` is never reached.

### Case 2: the property is owned (`_owners = { Fast Kebabs → Alice }`)

| Step | Value |
|---|---|
| `TryGetValue` | **true**, `owner = Alice` |
| `!true` | **false** |
| `if` block | **skipped** |
| `if (owner == player)` | runs next, with `owner = Alice` |

Then one of two things happens:
- **The player is Alice** (she landed on her own property) → `Alice == Alice` → `return`, and no rent is paid.
- **The player is Bob** → `Alice == Bob` is false → the code continues to the rent code.

## The whole method as a flow

```
Player lands on a property
        │
        ▼
Is it in _owners?  ──NO──►  Buy it, add to _owners, return
        │
       YES (owner is set)
        │
        ▼
Is owner == player?  ──YES──►  Own property, return
        │
        NO
        ▼
Pay rent to owner
```

## The same thing without `!`

If `!` is what makes this confusing, this version does exactly the same thing:

```csharp
if (_owners.TryGetValue(property, out var owner))
{
    // property IS owned → owner is set
    if (owner == player) return;
    // ...pay rent
}
else
{
    // property is NOT owned → buy it
    var paid = player.Pay(property.Price);
    if (paid == property.Price) _owners[property] = player;
}
```

Your version uses `!` to handle the "not owned" case first and `return` early, which keeps the rest of the method less nested.

One small note on your comment: "if purchased property is not in dict" would read more accurately as "if the property is not owned yet (not in the dictionary)". At that point it hasn't been purchased.

2. Does `GoSpace` match `PropertySpace`? → **no**, so `property` isn't set
3. `is not` → **true**
4. `if (true) return;` → the method exits

## How it knows the actual type

`_board[4]` returns its value typed as `Space`, the **declared** type. But every object in .NET also remembers the class it was **created** as, its **runtime** type. When you write `new PropertySpace { ... }`, that object is stored as a `PropertySpace` for good.

The `is` check looks at the **runtime** type:

```csharp
Space s = _board[4];

Console.WriteLine(s.GetType().Name);   // PropertySpace  ← the runtime type
// the declared type of s is still Space
```

So the check is effectively:

```
_board[4].GetType()  →  PropertySpace
Is PropertySpace the same as, or a subclass of, PropertySpace?  →  yes  →  match
```

```
_board[0].GetType()  →  GoSpace
Is GoSpace the same as, or a subclass of, PropertySpace?  →  no  →  no match
```

The "or a subclass of" part matters. If you later had `class Railway : PropertySpace`, a `Railway` would also match `is PropertySpace`.

## Why the cast is needed

```csharp
_board[4].Price          // compile error: Space has no 'Price'
property.Price           // works: property is typed as PropertySpace
```

The compiler only sees the declared type `Space`, so it won't let you use `Price`. The `is` pattern checks the runtime type, then gives you a new variable, `property`, that the compiler knows is a `PropertySpace`.

## See it yourself

Add this temporarily, just before the `if`:

```csharp
var current = _board[player.Position];
Console.WriteLine($"Position {player.Position}: {current.GetType().Name} - {current.Name}");
```

Output:

```
Position 0: GoSpace - GO
Position 4: PropertySpace - The Grand Tofu
```

content.text:
`[int index]` uses square brackets because `this[...]` declares an **indexer**, not a normal method. The square brackets are what let you write `_board[4]` instead of `_board.Get(4)`.

## Indexer vs method

```csharp
// Indexer: square brackets, name is always "this"
public Space this[int index] => _spaces[index];

// Normal method: round brackets, you pick the name
public Space GetSpace(int index) => _spaces[index];
```

How you call each one:

```csharp
var a = _board[4];            // indexer
var b = _board.GetSpace(4);   // method
```

Both return the same object. The indexer just lets your `Board` class be used **like a list or array**.

## Why the square brackets

The declaration matches how you'll use it:

| Declaration | Usage |
|---|---|
| `this[int index]` | `_board[4]` |
| `GetSpace(int index)` | `_board.GetSpace(4)` |

- **`this`** means "this object itself", so `_board[...]` puts the brackets directly on the object.
- **`[int index]`** works like a method parameter: the `4` inside `_board[4]` goes into `index`.

If you wrote `public Space this(int index)` with round brackets, it wouldn't compile. C# needs the square brackets to recognise an indexer.

## Substituting values

```csharp
_board[4]
   │
   ▼
this[int index]  →  index = 4
   │
   ▼
_spaces[index]   →  _spaces[4]  →  PropertySpace { "The Grand Tofu", 3, "Red" }
```

## Built-in types you already use work the same way

`List<T>` and `Dictionary<TKey, TValue>` have indexers too. That's why these work:

```csharp
_spaces[4]               // List<Space>'s indexer
_owners[property]        // Dictionary<PropertySpace, Player>'s indexer
```

Inside .NET they're declared roughly like this:

```csharp
public T this[int index] { get; set; }            // List<T>
public TValue this[TKey key] { get; set; }        // Dictionary<TKey, TValue>
```

So the index doesn't have to be an `int`. A dictionary uses its key type, which is why `_owners[property]` takes a `PropertySpace`.

## Read-only vs read/write

Your version uses `=>`, so it's **read-only**:

```csharp
public Space this[int index] => _spaces[index];

var s = _board[4];        // works
_board[4] = someSpace;    // compile error: there's no set
```

A read/write indexer would look like this:

```csharp
public Space this[int index]
{
    get => _spaces[index];
    set => _spaces[index] = value;
}
```

Read-only makes sense for a board, because nothing should replace spaces during a game.

content.text:
There's a small mix-up with the table. For `abstract` it says the **opposite**:

| Keyword | Can use `new`? | Can be inherited? |
|---|---|---|
| `abstract` | **no** | **yes (must be)** |

- **"Can use `new`?" → no:** you can't write `new Space()`.
- **"Can be inherited?" → yes (must be):** an abstract class is only useful if a child class inherits from it, because that's the only way to get an object.

So the "must be" was about **inheriting**, not creating objects.

## About `: base(...)`

One correction to your explanation: `: base(...)` does **not** create a separate object of the abstract class. Only **one** object is created, the child. `: base(...)` just runs the parent's **constructor** on that same object, to fill in the parent's part.

```csharp
public abstract class Space
{
    public string Name { get; }

    protected Space(string name)
    {
        Name = name;
    }
}

public sealed class PropertySpace : Space
{
    public int Price { get; }
    public string Colour { get; }

    public PropertySpace(string name, int price, string colour) : base(name)
    {
        Price = price;
        Colour = colour;
    }
}
```

```csharp
var p = new PropertySpace("Fast Kebabs", 2, "Brown");
```

### What happens, step by step

```
1. new PropertySpace(...)  → memory is set aside for ONE object
                             (room for Name + Price + Colour)

2. : base("Fast Kebabs")   → Space's constructor runs on that same object
                             Name = "Fast Kebabs"

3. PropertySpace body runs → Price = 2, Colour = "Brown"

4. Result: one object
   ┌───────────────────────────────┐
   │ PropertySpace object          │
   │  ├─ Name   = "Fast Kebabs"    │  ← the part from Space
   │  ├─ Price  = 2                │  ← the part from PropertySpace
   │  └─ Colour = "Brown"          │
   └───────────────────────────────┘
```

There's no separate `Space` object anywhere. The `PropertySpace` object **contains** the `Space` part.

### Proof

```csharp
var p = new PropertySpace("Fast Kebabs", 2, "Brown");
Space s = p;

Console.WriteLine(ReferenceEquals(p, s));   // True: same single object
Console.WriteLine(s.GetType().Name);         // PropertySpace, not Space
```

Even when you hold it as a `Space` variable, the object is still a `PropertySpace`.

## A good way to think of it

- **`abstract` class** = a **blueprint fragment**. It describes the shared parts (`Name`), but you can't build anything from it alone.
- **Child class** = the **complete blueprint**. It adds the rest (`Price`, `Colour`).
- **`new Child(...)`** = build **one** thing from the complete blueprint.
- **`: base(...)`** = while building it, run the fragment's setup steps for the shared parts.

That's also why abstract classes usually have `protected` constructors. Only child classes, through `: base(...)`, should call them, never `new` from outside.

content.text:
No. In C#, `==` on strings is **case-sensitive**, so `"Brown" == "brown"` is **false**.

```csharp
"Brown" == "Brown"   // true
"Brown" == "brown"   // false
"Brown" == "BROWN"   // false
```

## The fix

Use `string.Equals` with `StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase`:

```csharp
public List<PropertySpace> ColourGroup(string colour)
{
    return _spaces
        .OfType<PropertySpace>()
        .Where(space => string.Equals(space.Colour, colour, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase))
        .ToList();
}
```

```csharp
string.Equals("Brown", "brown", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)   // true
string.Equals("Brown", "BROWN", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)   // true
string.Equals("Brown", "Red",   StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)   // false
```

I'd use the static `string.Equals(a, b, ...)` rather than `space.Colour.Equals(colour, ...)`. The static version is safe if `Colour` is `null`, while `null.Equals(...)` would throw a `NullReferenceException`.

## Why it matters for rent

This bug can make rent come out **wrong**. Suppose `board.json` has:

```
Fast Kebabs   Colour = "Brown"
jamai         Colour = "brown"
```

Alice owns **only** Fast Kebabs. With the case-sensitive `==`:

```
ColourGroup("Brown")  →  [ Fast Kebabs ]      (jamai is left out)
.All(...)             →  Alice owns every item in the list → true
ownsGroup = true      →  rent is doubled
```

Alice gets double rent while owning only half the brown set. With `OrdinalIgnoreCase`, both properties are in the group, the check fails on jamai, and rent stays normal.

## Another approach

Instead of comparing ignoring case everywhere, you can **normalise the colour once** when the board is loaded, for example by making all colours lowercase. Then a plain `==` works everywhere. Changing the comparison in `ColourGroup` is the smaller fix, so I'd start there.

content.text:
Yes, your understanding is right. `!arg.StartsWith('-')` means **"the argument does NOT start with `-`"**.

## How to read it

The method call runs **first**, then `!` flips its result:

```
!arg.StartsWith('-')
     └──────┬──────┘
     step 1: arg.StartsWith('-')  → true or false
└─┬─┘
step 2: !  flips it               → false or true
```

So it's really:

```csharp
!(arg.StartsWith('-'))
```

`!` never applies to `arg` alone. It applies to the `bool` that `StartsWith` returns.

## Substituting values

`args = ["--json", "board.json", "rolls.json"]`

`Where` takes each `arg` in turn and keeps it only if the condition is **true**:

| `arg` | `arg.StartsWith('-')` | `!` result | Kept? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `"--json"` | true | **false** | no |
| `"board.json"` | false | **true** | yes |
| `"rolls.json"` | false | **true** | yes |

Result: `["board.json", "rolls.json"]`

## Comparing it with `!=`, which you already find easy

These two do the same kind of job, just in different places:

```csharp
arg != "--json"            // "arg is not equal to --json"
!arg.StartsWith('-')       // "arg does not start with -"
```

- `!=` is a comparison operator between two values.
- `!` before a method call flips the `true`/`false` that the method returns.

If the `!` version is hard to read, this is exactly the same:

```csharp
args.Where(arg => arg.StartsWith('-') == false)
```

`!x` and `x == false` mean the same thing. Most C# code uses `!`, but either works.

## A quick tip for reading `!`

When you see `!` followed by a method call, read it as **"not"** and then the method name as a sentence:

| Code | Read it as |
|---|---|
| `!arg.StartsWith('-')` | "arg does **not** start with -" |
| `!File.Exists(path)` | "the file does **not** exist" |
| `!_owners.TryGetValue(...)` | "the owners dictionary does **not** have it" |
| `!args.Contains("--json")` | "args does **not** contain --json" |

One small thing: `!==` is JavaScript. In C# it's just `!=`. You probably mixed them up because you have JavaScript code in this folder too.

content.text:
Name checking would work, but there's one catch first: your data files are named **`rolls_1.json`, `rolls_2.json` and `rolls_3.json`**, not `rolls.json`. If you require exactly `rolls.json`, your own files will be rejected. Any name check has to allow those numbered names.

## Option 1: string methods (simplest, no regex)

```csharp
var boardName = Path.GetFileName(paths[0]);   // "data\board.json"   → "board.json"
var rollsName = Path.GetFileName(paths[1]);   // "data\rolls_1.json" → "rolls_1.json"

var boardOk = boardName.StartsWith("board", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)
           && boardName.EndsWith(".json", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase);

var rollsOk = rollsName.StartsWith("rolls", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)
           && rollsName.EndsWith(".json", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase);

if (!boardOk || !rollsOk)
{
    Console.Error.WriteLine("Error: expected a board file first (board*.json), then a rolls file (rolls*.json)");
    return 2;
}
```

`Path.GetFileName` matters here. Users often pass `data\board.json`, and you only want to check the **name** part, not the folder.

| Command | `boardName` / `rollsName` | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `data\board.json data\rolls_1.json` | `board.json` / `rolls_1.json` | OK |
| `data\rolls_1.json data\board.json` | `rolls_1.json` / `board.json` | error (swapped) |
| `Board.JSON Rolls_2.json` | | OK (case ignored) |
| `board_backup.json rolls_old.json` | | OK (this check is loose) |

## Option 2: regex (stricter)

Use a regex when you want to define **exactly** which names are allowed. For example: `rolls.json` or `rolls_` followed by a number, and nothing else.

```csharp
using System.Text.RegularExpressions;

var boardOk = Regex.IsMatch(boardName, @"^board\.json$", RegexOptions.IgnoreCase);
var rollsOk = Regex.IsMatch(rollsName, @"^rolls(_\d+)?\.json$", RegexOptions.IgnoreCase);
```

The pattern `^rolls(_\d+)?\.json$` breaks down like this:

| Part | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `^` | start of the name |
| `rolls` | the literal text `rolls` |
| `(_\d+)?` | optionally, `_` followed by one or more digits |
| `\.json` | `.json` (the `\` makes `.` mean a real dot) |
| `$` | end of the name |

| Name | Matches? |
|---|---|
| `rolls.json` | yes |
| `rolls_1.json` | yes |
| `rolls_23.json` | yes |
| `rolls_old.json` | no (`old` isn't digits) |
| `myrolls_1.json` | no (doesn't start with `rolls`) |
| `rolls_1.json.bak` | no (doesn't end with `.json`) |

## Efficiency

Speed doesn't matter here. It's two short names checked once, so any approach takes microseconds. Choose for **readability and strictness**:

- **String methods:** easier to read, but loose.
- **Regex:** strict and precise, but harder to read if you're not used to regex.

## My recommendation

I'd **keep the content check (`LooksLikeRolls`) and not enforce file names**. Here's why:

1. **Names can be wrong while the contents are right.** If someone renames or copies the file, say `test_board.json`, a name check rejects a perfectly valid file.
2. **Names can be right while the contents are wrong.** `board.json` could contain rolls by mistake. A name check lets that through, and the content check catches it.
3. **Your usage message says `BOARD_FILE ROLLS_FILE`**, which promises any file name. A name rule would quietly break that promise.

If you still want a name check, use the **regex** version, because it's the only one that's actually strict. Use it **as well as** the content check, not instead of it. And put the expected pattern in the usage message so users know the rule:

```
Usage: dotnet run -- board.json rolls_N.json [--json]
```

content.text:
For a coding interview, I'd go with **neither name check**. Rely on **content validation**, and if you do add a name check, use string methods rather than regex.

## Why not regex here

In an interview you'll be asked to **explain every line you wrote**. If you can't comfortably explain `^rolls(_\d+)?\.json$` on the spot, it will hurt more than it helps. Interviewers don't reward clever code you can't explain. They reward code you **understand and can defend**.

## Why not name checks at all

An interviewer may well ask: *"What if I rename the file to `test_board.json`?"* With a name check, your program rejects a valid file, and that's hard to defend. With content checks, the honest answer is easy:

> "I don't trust file names. I validate what's inside each file, so a swapped or wrong file is caught no matter what it's called."

That's a strong answer and shows good engineering judgment.

## What to do instead

Make your **loaders** give clear errors. Then a swapped file is caught naturally, with no extra checks in `Program.cs`:

```
dotnet run -- data\rolls_1.json data\board.json

Error: board file must be a JSON array of spaces (objects with "name" and "type")
```

If `Board.Load` and `Game.LoadRolls` already throw `GameInputException` with messages like that, you're covered. `LooksLikeRolls` is a nice extra that gives a friendlier "the files look swapped" message. It's optional.

## What to say in the interview

If they ask about argument handling, something like:

> "I check for unknown options and the right number of paths, check that the files exist, and validate each file's contents when loading. I chose not to enforce file names, because names are easy to change and don't prove what's inside. Content validation catches swapped or wrong files no matter what they're called."

That covers everything you listed (duplicate `--json`, unknown options, missing files, the same file twice and swapped files) using only `StartsWith`, `Count`, `File.Exists` and `Path.GetFullPath`. You understand all of those, and you can explain each one.

There's no real efficiency gain to chase here, since it's only a few strings. What matters is keeping them in **one place** and making sure nothing else depends on them.

## What I'd do

Define the names once:

```csharp
public static class GameRules
{
    // Replace these with the names and order from the brief
    public static readonly IReadOnlyList<string> PlayerNames =
        new[] { "Player1", "Player2", "Player3", "Player4" };
}
```

Pass them into `Game`, instead of having `Game` create them itself:

```csharp
public Game(Board board, IReadOnlyList<int> rolls, IEnumerable<string> playerNames)
{
    _board = board;
    _rolls = rolls;
    _players = playerNames.Select(name => new Player(name)).ToList();
}
```

Then supply them in `Program.cs`:

```csharp
var result = new Game(board, rolls, GameRules.PlayerNames).Play();
```

Your `Player` constructor may look different, so adjust that line to match.

## Why this is better

- **Easy to change:** new names or a different player count only need one edit.
- **Easy to test:** a test can pass its own players, such as `new Game(board, rolls, new[] { "A", "B" })`.
- **No hidden "4":** choosing the next player doesn't rely on a fixed count:

```csharp
var player = _players[turn % _players.Count];
```

These are the things to check for in your code, because they'd break on a different board or rolls file:

| Don't hard-code | Use instead |
|---|---|
| Board size, such as `% 9` | `_board.Count` |
| Number of rolls | Loop until the rolls run out or the game ends |
| Property names or colours, such as `"Brown"` | Values read from the board file |
| Position of GO, such as `Position == 0` for a special case | The space's type (`GoSpace`), if the board could be ordered differently |
| Expected winners or final scores | Calculate them from the game |

Good call, but add one more condition: **the whole number must also be 1 or greater**. A whole number check alone would let `0` and `-1` through, and a player can't move zero or negative spaces.

You can do both checks together while reading each roll:

```csharp
var rolls = new List<int>();

foreach (var item in doc.RootElement.EnumerateArray())
{
    if (item.ValueKind != JsonValueKind.Number
        || !item.TryGetInt32(out var roll)
        || roll < 1)
    {
        throw new GameInputException(
            $"Invalid roll {item}: a roll must be a whole number of 1 or greater");
    }

    rolls.Add(roll);
}
```

The conditions run in order, and the first one that's true triggers the error:

| Value | Number? | Whole number? | 1 or greater? | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `4` | yes | yes | yes | accepted |
| `7` | yes | yes | yes | accepted |
| `"abc"` | **no** | not checked | not checked | error |
| `2.5` | yes | **no** | not checked | error |
| `0` | yes | yes | **no** | error |
| `-1` | yes | yes | **no** | error |

The `ValueKind` check has to come first, because `TryGetInt32` throws an `InvalidOperationException` on a non-number instead of returning `false`.

I can't see your `LoadRolls`, so adjust the variable names to match it. It also assumes you've already confirmed the file is a JSON array, because `EnumerateArray()` throws on anything else.

content.text:
`Any` only returns `true` or `false`, so it can't give you the index. The simplest replacement is `FindIndex`, which works on a list:

```csharp
var stringIndex = doc.RootElement
    .EnumerateArray()
    .ToList()
    .FindIndex(item => item.ValueKind == JsonValueKind.String);
```

It returns the index of the **first** match, or **`-1`** if nothing matches:

| JSON | `stringIndex` |
|---|---|
| `[1, 2, 3]` | -1 |
| `[1, "abc", 3]` | 1 |
| `["x", 2, "y"]` | 0 (only the first match) |

Then use it like this:

```csharp
if (stringIndex != -1)
{
    throw new GameInputException($"Invalid roll at position {stringIndex}: it is a string");
}
```

## Getting every string's index

`Select` can pass each item's index along with the item:

```csharp
var stringIndexes = doc.RootElement
    .EnumerateArray()
    .Select((item, index) => new { item, index })
    .Where(x => x.item.ValueKind == JsonValueKind.String)
    .Select(x => x.index)
    .ToList();
```

For `["x", 2, "y"]`, this gives `[0, 2]`. If there are no strings, you get an empty list.

For your validation, use `FindIndex`, since stopping at the first bad value is enough and it's easier to explain in an interview.

content.text:
Yes: **accept "Banana" as a valid colour**. The game never uses colour as an actual colour. It only uses it to answer "which properties belong to the same group?", so "Banana" works just as well as "Brown", as long as the properties in that group share the same value.

That means there's no need for a list of valid colours, and your code stays free of hard-coded values. The brief also says hidden boards can have different colour groups, so a fixed list could reject valid boards.

## What to validate instead

Check that the colour is **usable as a group label**: it must exist, be a string and not be blank.

```csharp
if (!item.TryGetProperty("colour", out var colourElement)
    || colourElement.ValueKind != JsonValueKind.String
    || string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(colourElement.GetString()))
{
    throw new GameInputException($"Space at position {index} must have a non-empty colour");
}

var colour = colourElement.GetString()!.Trim();
```

Use this only for property spaces, because GO has no colour. Change `"colour"` and `index` if your loader uses different names. Check the exact key against your `board.json`.

| Colour value | Result |
|---|---|
| `"Brown"` | accepted |
| `"Banana"` | accepted, as its own colour group |
| `" Brown "` | accepted, and `Trim()` makes it `"Brown"` |
| `""` or `"   "` | error |
| `5` or `null` | error |
| key missing | error |

`Trim()` matters because `"Brown "` would otherwise become a separate group from `"Brown"`, which could wrongly double the rent.

## What happens with "Banana"

If only one property is "Banana", it forms a group of one, so its owner always has the full set and charges double rent. That matches your existing assumption at [README.md:51](woven_monopoly/README.md:51).

A typo like `"Brwon"` can't be detected, because it looks like any other new colour. It would simply create its own group of one, so mention that limit in your README:

> **Colours:** A colour is treated as a group label, so any non-empty text is valid, including values like "Banana". Colours are compared ignoring case and surrounding spaces. I don't keep a list of allowed colours because the brief says not to hard-code details from the sample files, so a misspelt colour creates a separate group.

content.text:
That's a fair reason, and it's a better argument than saying `%` is uncommon. Your version does keep the two jobs separate: `turn` picks the roll, and `currentIndex` picks the player. If you expect to change the bankruptcy rules, **keep it**.

Two of those claims go a bit too far, so avoid them if you're asked:

- **"The rolls and turn would have to change":** with `turn % count`, only the player selection would change, because `_rolls[turn]` works either way.
- **"Open for extension":** this usually means adding behaviour without editing existing code, but removing players would still mean editing `Play()`. "Easier to extend" is more accurate.

Here's the wording for your README:

> **Turn order:** I track the current player with `currentIndex` instead of using `_players[turn % _players.Count]`. This separates the two jobs: `turn` selects the roll, and `currentIndex` selects the player. The game currently ends at the first bankruptcy, so nobody is removed from `activePlayers`, and the simpler formula would work today. I accepted the extra variables because this approach is easier to extend. If bankrupt players later stay out while the game continues, only the bankruptcy handling needs to change: remove the player and wrap `currentIndex` if needed. The roll selection stays the same.

That wording admits the trade-off and explains why you accepted it, which is what an interviewer will want to hear. If they ask why you didn't use the shorter formula, you can say:

> "Today it would work, and it's shorter. I chose this because bankruptcy rules were the change I thought most likely, and it only costs a couple of extra variables."

# Woven Monopoly (C#)

Run from this directory:

```powershell
dotnet run -- board.json rolls_1.json --json
dotnet run -- board.json rolls_2.json --json
```

To print a readable summary, omit `--json`. The app requires the .NET 10 SDK and uses only the .NET standard library; there are no third-party dependencies.

## Language choice

I understand team uses Ruby, but I chose to implement the solution in C#. I’m still learning Ruby, and building the initial version in a language I’m fluent in helps me:
-understand the problem domain clearly
-validate the behaviour against the JSON input format
-ensure the board, spaces, and movement logic are correct
-produce an implementation I can confidently explain
This approach lets me focus on correctness and clarity before handling with Ruby syntax and idiom

## Design

- `Board` loads and validates the board, stores its spaces in order, and handles circular movement and GO passes.
- `Game` manages turn order, money, ownership, rent, receivable and the stopping condition.
- `Player` owns the player's balance and payment behavior.
- `GameResult` contains the final outcome and formats the readable summary. The CLI is in `Program.cs`.

The board can have any number of spaces and colour groups. Rent doubles when an owner has every property in that colour group.

## Assumptions

- A player who cannot pay a purchase price or rent pays their remaining cash, becomes bankrupt, and the game stops immediately. The property is not transferred when the player cannot afford to buy it.
- If the rolls run out before bankruptcy, the player or players with the most money win. Equal balances are reported as a tie.
- Passing GO multiple times in a single move pays the bonus once per pass. Landing on GO exactly counts as passing it; the initial position does not.
- Rent equals the property’s price and double it when one owner holds every property of that colour, but it doesn’t give a base rent in the board.json. I used the property price to calculate the rent because it’s the only amount the board provides. For example, a $3 property costs $3 in rent, or $6 if the owner holds the full colour set.
- Partial payment causes bankruptcy.
- Rolls: The requirement did not mention anything about no. of dice. The provided roll files only contain 1 to 6, which fits a single six-sided die, but I don’t enforce a maximum. This avoids hard-coding a limit taken from the sample files. Any whole number of 1 or greater is accepted.
- A roll must be a whole number of 1 or greater, and no maximum is enforced. Zero and negative rolls are rejected as invalid input, because a dice roll can’t produce them. Players therefore only move forward, and backward movement isn’t implemented.
- Gospace assumption must contain one go space

## Review findings by Me

- All the Catch in the coding was identified and implemented by me. I have analysed the AI Generated code base found bugs, handled exception, modified some of the code and implemnted them in a simple way

- Turn order: In Game.cs - Play method - I track the current player with currentIndex instead of AI - Suggested using \_players[turn % _players.Count]. This separates the two jobs: turn selects the roll, and currentIndex selects the player.
  Turn Order Handling - Bug found with AI suggested version

               //the order is Peter, Billy, Charlotte and Sweedal:
                Turn 5: 5 % 4 = 1 → Billy (bankrupt)
                    Remove Billy
                Turn 6: 6 % 3 = 0 → Peter <<ideally it should be Charlotte not Peter>>
                Turn 7: 7 % 3 = 1 → Charlotte
                Turn 8: 8 % 3 = 2 → Sweedal
                Turn 9: 9 % 3 = 0 → Peter

The game currently ends at the first bankruptcy, so nobody is removed from activePlayers, and the simpler formula would work today. I introduced extra variables because this approach is easier to extend. If bankrupt players later stay out while the game continues, only the bankruptcy handling needs to change: remove the player and wrap currentIndex if needed. The roll selection stays the same. Separation of concerns.

- I designed each Game instance to represent one complete game. This prevents accidentally replaying the same instance with previously accumulated money, player positions, and property ownership. If we need to play another game, we can create a new Game instance.
- In program.cs the file related check condition were not identified and implemented by AI.
  When I reviewed I could find possible ways the application could crash or the exception go
  unhandled. The followeing checks were implemented by me:
  1. What if the user swap board.json and roll.json, eg. dotnet run rolls.json board.json
     is handled because the Board.cs expects and can only handle data from board.json. If unhandled this will crash the application at the RUN time.
  2. Multiple --json option are and unknown --json options are handled in the code.
  3. No 2 path of the argument are same, this ensure both the files are different. eg. dotnet run board.json board.json --json will throw Error: BOARD_FILE and ROLLS_FILE must be different files
- In Board.cs .json could be Empty Array [] AI did not check and I reviewed and implemented this

- A colour is treated as a group label, so any non-empty text is valid, including values like “Banana”. Colours are compared ignoring case and surrounding spaces. No Valid color are checked to avoid hard-code details from the sample files, so a misspelt colour creates a separate group. Eg. "Brown" != "brown" fixed it by ignoreCase, " Brown " fixed by Trimmin

`rolls_3.json` is `[1,3,4,5,1,1,6,1,1,1]`. Before running it, I expected Peter to buy both Brown properties on turns 1 and 5. Charlotte starts turn 7 on space 4; a roll of 6 wraps her to The Burvale (space 1), where Peter owns the complete Brown group. She should pay Peter doubled rent of $2. The remaining three rolls continue the game without changing that scenario.

- In program.cs the file related check condition were not identified and implemented by AI.
  When I reviewed I could find possible ways the application could crash or the exception go
  unhandled. The followeing checks were implemented by me:
  1. What if the user swap board.json and roll.json, eg. dotnet run rolls.json board.json
     is handled because the Board.cs expects and can only handle data from board.json. If unhandled this will crash the application at the RUN time.
  2. Multiple --json option are and unknown --json options are handled in the code.
  3. No 2 path of the argument are same, this ensure both the files are different. eg. dotnet run board.json board.json --json will throw Error: BOARD_FILE and ROLLS_FILE must be different files
- In Board.cs .json could be Empty Array [] AI did not check and I reviewed and implemented this

- A colour is treated as a group label, so any non-empty text is valid, including values like “Banana”. Colours are compared ignoring case and surrounding spaces. No Valid color are checked to avoid hard-code details from the sample files, so a misspelt colour creates a separate group. Eg. "Brown" != "brown" fixed it by ignoreCase, " Brown " fixed by Trimmin

## Hand-designed game

`rolls_3.json` is `[1,3,4,5,1,1,6,1,1,1]`. Before running it, I expected Peter to buy both Brown properties on turns 1 and 5. Charlotte starts turn 7 on space 4; a roll of 6 wraps her to The Burvale (space 1), where Peter owns the complete Brown group. She should pay Peter doubled rent of $2. The remaining three rolls continue the game without changing that scenario.

# Woven coding test
 
Your task is to write a program that plays the game of Woven Monopoly.
 
In Woven Monopoly the dice rolls are set ahead of time, so the game is deterministic.
 
## Game rules
 
* There are four players who take turns in the following order:
  * Peter
  * Billy
  * Charlotte
  * Sweedal
* Each player starts with $16
* Everybody starts on GO
* You get $1 when you pass GO (this excludes your starting move)
* If you land on a property, you must buy it
* If you land on an owned property, you must pay rent to the owner
* If the same owner owns all property of the same colour, the rent is doubled
* Once someone is bankrupt, whoever has the most money remaining is the winner
* There are no chance cards, jail or stations
* The board wraps around (when you reach the last space, the next space is the first space)
 
## What to build
 
* Load the board from `board.json`
* Implement the game logic as per the rules
* Load the dice rolls from `rolls_1.json` and `rolls_2.json` and simulate each game. For each game, report:
  * Who wins
  * How much money each player ends up with
  * Which space each player finishes on
 
## How we will run your program
 
We will run your program ourselves, including against boards and roll files you haven't seen. They follow the same formats as the files in this pack, but boards can have a different number of spaces and colour groups of different sizes, and roll files can be any length. Please don't hard-code anything about the sample files.
 
Your program must:
 
* Take the path to a board file and the path to a rolls file as its two arguments
* Accept a `--json` flag that prints the result to standard output in this shape (extra fields are fine):
 
```json
{
  "winners": ["Peter"],
  "players": [
    { "name": "Peter", "money": 20, "space": "Massizim" },
    { "name": "Billy", "money": 12, "space": "GO" },
    { "name": "Charlotte", "money": 9, "space": "YOMG" },
    { "name": "Sweedal", "money": 3, "space": "The Burvale" }
  ]
}
```
 
`winners` is a list so that you can report a tie. The numbers above are an example of the format, not the answer.
 
Put the exact command to run it at the top of your README, for example `bin/woven_monopoly board.json rolls_1.json --json`. Without `--json`, print whatever human-readable summary you think is most useful.
 
## Gaps in the rules
 
The rules leave some situations open. Real requirements usually do, so this is on purpose. Where you find a gap, make a sensible decision, implement it consistently, and record it in an **ASSUMPTIONS** section of your README with a sentence on why you chose it.
 
If you would rather ask than assume, email [contact email]. Asking questions never counts against you.
 
## Using AI
 
We expect you to use AI tools and we encourage it. We are interested in how you direct them and how you check their work, so we won't mark you down for the amount of code an AI wrote.
 
Please include an `AI_USAGE.md` file that covers:
 
* Which tools you used, and what you used each one for
* At least two places where a tool was wrong, unhelpful or over-complicated things, how you noticed, and what you did about it
* Something you decided to write or rewrite yourself, and why
 
If your tool can export its sessions or chat history (Cursor and Claude Code both can), include the exports in an `ai-sessions/` folder. Remove anything personal first.
 
## Design your own test game
 
Add a `rolls_3.json` file that you have designed by hand to produce a particular situation in the game. In your README, explain what it tests and what result you expect, worked out before you ran your program. Keep it short: 10 to 30 rolls is plenty.
 
## Language
 
We are a Ruby team (we run JRuby in production, so code compatible with Ruby 3.1 is ideal). Ruby is preferred. If you choose another language, tell us why in your README.
 
## Scope and time
 
* Plan on 2 to 3 hours. If you go over, stop and note in your README what you would do next
* This is a command-line program: no user interface, database or web framework
* Keep third-party dependencies to testing and linting tools
 
## What we are looking for
 
* Code that is well thought out and tested
* Clean and readable code
* Extensibility, since the rules will change
* A git history with small changes committed often, so we can see your approach
 
Please approach this as you would a production problem, using whatever approach to coding and testing you think is appropriate.
 
## What to submit
 
* Your source code, including the `.git` folder (a zip of the repository or a link to it)
* A README with:
  * How to install dependencies, run the tests and run the program
  * Your design decisions
  * Your ASSUMPTIONS section
  * The output of your program for `rolls_1.json` and `rolls_2.json`
* `AI_USAGE.md`, and `ai-sessions/` if you have exports
* `rolls_3.json`, with its explanation in your README
 
## What happens next
 
If we progress with your application, we will book a 60-minute session with you. You will walk us through your code, make a small change to it, and extend it with a new rule using your usual tools, including AI. Part of the session is without AI assistance, so make sure you are comfortable explaining and changing your own code. Please have your development environment ready to share your screen.

Write it as an **assumption**, because you're deciding how the program behaves in a case the rules don't settle. You can still mention the test in your review notes, but the `ASSUMPTIONS` section is where the decision belongs.

Before you keep the check, there's a catch: [TASK_BRIEF.md:35](woven_monopoly/data/TASK_BRIEF.md:35) says "roll files can be any length". Read literally, that could include an empty file, and they'll run files you haven't seen. "Set ahead of time" only means the rolls are fixed in advance, so it doesn't rule out an empty list.

## What I'd do

This is a good one to email them about, since the brief says asking never counts against you:

> Should an empty rolls file (`[]`) be rejected as invalid, or played as a game with no turns?

**If you don't get an answer, I'd accept it and remove the check.** Nobody moves, so all four players tie on $16 at GO. That's a valid result, while rejecting the file would be an error if their test includes it.

| Your decision | README wording |
|---|---|
| **Accept `[]`** | An empty rolls file is valid, because the brief says roll files can be any length. No turns are played, so all players tie with their starting money. |
| **Reject `[]`** | An empty rolls file is rejected as invalid input. The brief says roll files can be any length, but I treat a game with no rolls as a mistake in the input, because no game would actually be played. |

Rejecting is still defensible if you prefer it, as long as you record the reason. If you keep your check, put it **after** the array check, because `GetArrayLength()` throws `InvalidOperationException` on anything that isn't an array.

## Your other comments

- **Catch 7:** it still says a float throws `InvalidOperationException`. Only non-numbers like strings throw. For a float like `2.5`, `TryGetInt32` returns `false`.
- **Your `2.0` test:** I expect `TryGetInt32` to return `false`, which would show your "not a positive whole number" error, but your test will confirm it. If it's rejected, you could add this assumption: "A roll must be written as a whole number, so `2.0` is rejected."
